Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Overview</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">We are an independent oil and gas company engaged in development, production and acquisition activities primarily in the Rocky Mountains region of the United States where we are focused on developing our large resource play in the Williston Basin of North Dakota and Montana. &#160;As a result of the sharp decline in commodity prices during 2020 as well as our chapter 11 reorganization, we have significantly decreased our level of capital spending to more closely align with our reduced cash flows from operating activities. &#160;We have concentrated our capital program on projects that are expected to generate acceptable rates of return in the current price environment. &#160;We continually evaluate our property portfolio and sell properties when we believe that the sales price realized will provide an above average rate of return for the property or when the property no longer matches the profile of properties we desire to own. &#160;Refer to the &#8220;Acquisitions and Divestitures&#8221; footnote in the notes to the consolidated financial statements for more information on our recent acquisition and divestiture activity.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our revenue, profitability, cash flows and future growth rate depend on many factors which are beyond our control, such as oil and gas prices, economic, political and regulatory developments, the financial condition of our industry partners, competition from other sources of energy, and the other items discussed under the caption &#8220;Risk Factors&#8221; in Item&#160;1A of this Annual Report on Form&#160;10-K. &#160;Oil and gas prices historically have been volatile and may fluctuate widely in the future. style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt;"><span style="margin-bottom:12pt;visibility:hidden;">&#8203;</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Oil prices declined sharply during 2020 primarily in response to Saudi Arabia&#8217;s announcement of plans to abandon previously agreed upon output restraints and the economic effects of the coronavirus (&#8220;COVID-19&#8221;) pandemic on the demand for oil and natural gas. &#160;While prices began to recover in the second half of 2020, uncertainties related to demand for oil and natural gas products remain as the pandemic continues to impact the world economy. &#160;Lower oil, NGL and natural gas prices may not only decrease our revenues but may also reduce the amount of oil and natural gas that we can produce economically which decreases our oil and gas reserve quantities. &#160;Substantial and extended declines in oil, NGL and natural gas prices have resulted, and may result, in impairments of our proved oil and gas properties or undeveloped acreage (such as the impairments discussed below under &#8220;Results of Operations&#8221;) and may materially and adversely affect our future business, financial condition, cash flows, results of operations, liquidity or ability to fund planned capital expenditures. &#160;In addition, lower commodity prices may reduce the amount of our borrowing base under our credit agreement, which is determined at the discretion of our lenders and is based on the collateral value of our proved reserves that have been mortgaged to the lenders. &#160;Upon a redetermination, if borrowings in excess of the revised borrowing capacity were outstanding, we could be forced to immediately repay a portion of the debt outstanding under our credit agreement. &#160;Alternatively, higher oil prices may result in significant mark-to-market losses being incurred on our commodity-based derivatives.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">For a discussion of material changes to our proved reserves from December&#160;31, 2019 to December&#160;31, 2020 and our ability to convert PUDs to proved developed reserves, refer to &#8220;Reserves&#8221; in Item&#160;2 of this Annual Report on Form&#160;10-K. &#160;Additionally, for a discussion relating to the minimum remaining terms of our leases, refer to &#8220;Acreage&#8221; in Item&#160;2 of this Annual Report on Form&#160;10-K.</p></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div style="display:table-cell;vertical-align:bottom;width:100%;"><p and the effects of the implementation of the Plan, the consolidated financial statements after September&#160;1, 2020 are not comparable with the consolidated financial statements on or prior to that report on our results for the Successor Period and the Current Predecessor YTD Period separately, in certain circumstances management views our operating results for the year ended December&#160;31, 2020 by combining the results of the applicable Predecessor and Successor periods in order to provide the most meaningful comparison of our current results to prior periods. &#160;Accordingly, 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Settlement of Bankruptcy Claims. &#160;</i>Prior to the Chapter 11 Cases, WOG was party to various executory contracts with BNN Western, LLC, subsequently renamed Tallgrass Water Western, LLC (&#8220;Tallgrass&#8221;), including a Produced Water Gathering and Disposal Agreement (the &#8220;PWA&#8221;). &#160;In January 2021, WOG and Tallgrass entered into a settlement agreement to resolve all of the related claims before the Bankruptcy Court relating to such executory contracts, terminated the PWA and entered into a new Water Transport, Gathering and Disposal Agreement. &#160;In accordance with the settlement agreement, we made a $2 million cash payment and issued 948,897 shares of the Successor&#8217;s common stock pursuant to the confirmed Plan to a Tallgrass entity in February 2021.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">2020 Highlights and Future Considerations</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Operational Highlights</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="text-decoration:underline;text-decoration-color:#000000;">Operational Response to Market Conditions</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">As a result of the significant decline in crude oil prices during 2020 as well as our bankruptcy filing, we suspended all drilling and completion activity and terminated our drilling rig contracts in April 2020, incurring insignificant early termination and demobilization fees. &#160;Additionally, we curtailed production from certain of our producing wells, reduced the number of workover rigs operating on our properties, deferred the completion of certain wells and delayed placing some of our completed wells online during the second quarter of 2020. &#160;During the second half of 2020, we resumed workover and completion activity. &#160;In February 2021, we resumed drilling activity in the Williston Basin as further described below. &#160;Substantial and extended declines in crude oil prices may result in our decision to voluntarily curtail production or change the timing of when wells are placed online in the future. &#160;</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="text-decoration:underline;">North Dakota &amp; Montana&#160;&#8211; Williston Basin</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our properties in the Williston Basin of North Dakota and Montana target the Bakken and Three Forks formations. &#160;Net production from North Dakota and Montana averaged 83.2 MBOE/d for the fourth quarter of 2020, representing a 2% decrease from the third quarter of 2020. &#160;During the fourth quarter of 2020, we had one completion crew and turned-in-line 5 gross (3.9 net) wells in this area. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">In February 2021, we added a drilling rig in this area and currently plan to add a second rig in October 2021. &#160;We plan to continue with one completion crew in the area for the majority of 2021. &#160;Under our current 2021 capital program, we expect to TIL approximately 56 gross (36.8 net) wells in this area during the year.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="text-decoration:underline;">Colorado&#160;&#8211; Denver-Julesburg Basin</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our properties in the Denver-Julesburg Basin (&#8220;DJ Basin&#8221;) in Weld County, Colorado produce from the Niobrara &#8220;A,&#8221; &#8220;B&#8221; and &#8220;C&#8221; zones and the Codell/Fort Hays formations. &#160;Net production from Colorado averaged 8.2 MBOE/d in the fourth quarter of 2020, representing a 7% decrease from the third quarter of 2020. &#160;During 2020, we completed and turned-in-line 2 gross (1.9 net) wells in this area to test further extents of our acreage.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Financing Highlights</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">On the Emergence Date, in connection with our emergence from the Chapter 11 Cases, we repaid all outstanding borrowings and accrued interest on the Predecessor&#8217;s credit agreement (the &#8220;Predecessor Credit Agreement&#8221;) and entered into the Exit Credit Agreement<span style="background-color:#ffffff;">. &#160;Refer to &#8220;Recent Developments&#8221; above and the </span>&#8220;Long-Term Debt&#8221; footnote in the notes to the consolidated financial statements for more information.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Additionally, on the Emergence Date, we issued 36,817,630 shares of the Successor&#8217;s common stock to the holders of our outstanding senior notes in settlement of the outstanding principal and related accrued interest. &#160;Upon such settlement, we recognized a $1 billion gain in reorganization items, net. &#160;Refer to the &#8220;Fresh Start Accounting&#8221; footnote in the notes to the consolidated financial statements for more information. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">In March 2020, we paid $53 million to repurchase $73 million aggregate principal amount of our 1.25% Convertible Senior Notes due April 1, 2020 (the &#8220;Convertible Senior Notes&#8221;), which payment consisted of the average 72.5% purchase price plus all accrued and unpaid interest on the notes. &#160;We financed the repurchases with borrowings under the Predecessor Credit Agreement. &#160;Additionally, in March 2020, holders of $3 million aggregate principal amount of Convertible Senior Notes timely elected to convert. &#160;Upon such conversion, the holders of these notes were entitled to receive an insignificant cash payment on April&#160;1, 2020, which we did not pay in conjunction with the filing of the Chapter 11 Cases. &#160;Refer to the &#8220;Chapter 11 Emergence&#8221; and &#8220;Long-Term Debt&#8221; footnotes in the notes to the consolidated financial statements for more information on these repurchases and conversions. </p></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div <div style="background-color:#000000;clear:both;height:2pt;page-break-after:always;width:88.24%;border:0;margin:30pt 5.88% 30pt 5.88%;"></div><div style="max-width:100%;padding-left:5.88%;padding-right:5.88%;position:relative;"><div style="margin-top:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">2021 Exploration and Development Budget</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our 2021 exploration and development (&#8220;E&amp;D&#8221;) budget is a range of $228 million to $252 million, which we expect to fund with net cash provided by our operating activities and cash on hand, and represents a slight increase from the $209 million incurred on E&amp;D expenditures during the Combined Current YTD Period. &#160;This slight increase in spending is primarily attributable to our commitment to closely align capital spending with cash flows generated from operations and strict adherence to economic full cycle well returns. &#160;To the extent net cash provided by operating activities is higher or lower than currently anticipated, we would generate more or less free cash flow than we currently anticipate, and may adjust our E&amp;D budget or adjust borrowings outstanding under the Exit Credit Agreement. &#160;Approximately 94% of our 2021 E&amp;D budget is currently allocated to drilling and completion activity. &#160;We believe our 2021 E&amp;D plan provides the opportunity for the highest return and most efficient use of our capital on our existing development opportunities.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Acquisition and Divestiture Highlights</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="background-color:#ffffff;">On January&#160;9, 2020, we completed the divestiture of our interests in 30 non-operated, producing oil and gas wells and related undeveloped acreage located in McKenzie County, North Dakota for aggregate sales proceeds of $25 million (before closing adjustments). &#160;The divested properties consisted of less than 1% of our estimated proved reserves as of December&#160;31, 2019 and 1% of our average daily production for the year ended December&#160;31, 2019.</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="background-color:#ffffff;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Dakota Access Pipeline</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="background-color:#ffffff;">On March 25, 2020, the U.S. District Court for D.C. (&#8220;D.C. District Court&#8221;) found that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers had violated the National Environmental Policy Act when it granted an easement relating to a portion of the DAPL because it had failed to prepare an environmental impact statement. &#160;As a result, in an order issued July 6, 2020, the D.C. District Court vacated the easement and directed that the DAPL be shut down and emptied of oil by August 5, 2020. &#160;On August 5, 2020, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (&#8220;D.C. Appellate Court&#8221;) granted a stay of the portion of the order directing the shutdown of the DAPL. &#160;The stay allowed the DAPL to continue to operate until a further ruling was made. &#160;On January 26, 2021, the D.C. Appellate Court affirmed the D.C. District Court&#8217;s decision to vacate the easement and concluded that the D.C. District Court must further consider whether shut down of the DAPL is an appropriate remedy while the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers develops an environmental impact statement. &#160;We cannot provide any assurance as to the ultimate outcome of the litigation, and it is possible the DAPL may be required to be shut down as a result of such litigation. &#160;The disruption of transportation as a result of the DAPL being shut down or the anticipation of DAPL being shut down could negatively impact our ability to achieve the most favorable prices for our crude oil production, which could have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations or cash flows. &#160;To mitigate the potential impact of an unfavorable ruling, we are coordinating with our midstream partners and downstream markets to source transportation alternatives.</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><span style="background-color:#ffffff;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Restructuring</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">During September 2020, we executed a workforce reduction as part of an organizational redesign and cost reduction strategy to better align our business with the current operating environment and drive long-term value. &#160;We incurred a one-time net charge related to this restructuring of $8&#160;million, which was recorded to general and administrative expenses in the consolidated statements of operations during the Successor Period. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt;"><span style="font-weight:bold;visibility:hidden;">&#8203;</span></p></div><div <div style="background-color:#000000;clear:both;height:2pt;page-break-after:always;width:88.24%;border:0;margin:30pt 5.88% 30pt 5.88%;"></div><div style="max-width:100%;padding-left:5.88%;padding-right:5.88%;position:relative;"><div style="margin-top:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt;"><a href="#TOC"><span style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;text-align:left;">Table of Contents</span></a></p></div><div style="clear:both;max-width:100%;position:relative;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Successor Period and Current YTD Predecessor Period or Combined Current YTD Period Compared to Prior Predecessor YTD Period</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Oil, NGL and Natural Gas Sales</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>Our oil, NGL and natural gas sales revenue decreased $840 million to $732 million when comparing the Combined Current YTD Period to the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;Changes in sales revenue between periods are due to changes in production volumes sold and changes in average commodity prices realized (excluding the impacts of hedging). &#160;For the Combined Current YTD Period, decreases in total production accounted for approximately $395 million of the change in revenue and decreases in realized prices accounted for approximately $445 million of the change in revenue when compared to the Prior Predecessor YTD Period.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:12pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our oil, NGL and gas volumes decreased 26%, 13% and 13%, respectively, during the Combined Current YTD Period compared to the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;The volume decreases between periods were primarily attributable to operational decisions to curtail production, reduce drilling and workover activity, defer completions of certain wells and delay placing some of our completed wells online during the majority of the Combined Current YTD Period as described in &#8220;Operational Response to Market Conditions&#8221; above, as well as normal field production decline. &#160;These decreases were partially offset by increased production from new wells drilled and completed over the last twelve months in the Williston Basin. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our average price for oil, NGLs and natural gas (before the effects of hedging) decreased 37%, 27% and 81%, respectively, between periods primarily due to decreases in commodity market prices. &#160;Our average sales price realized for NGLs and natural gas during the Current Predecessor YTD Period was negatively impacted by high fixed third-party costs for transportation, gathering and compression services. &#160;These third-party costs sometimes exceed the ultimate price we receive for our natural gas and accordingly can result in negative gas revenues, which occurred during the Current Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;While these negative gas prices adversely affect our total revenues, we have continued to produce our wells in order to sell the associated oil and NGLs from these wells and to meet lease and regulatory requirements. &#160;Our average sales price realized for NGLs and natural gas improved during the Successor Period due to seasonal increases in market prices. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Lease Operating Expenses</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>Our lease operating expenses (&#8220;LOE&#8221;) during the Combined Current YTD Period were $232 million, a $96 million decrease over the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;This decrease was primarily due to (i) cost reduction initiatives which were implemented beginning in the third quarter of 2019 which contributed to a $59 million decrease in LOE and (ii) a $37 million decrease in saltwater disposal costs due to reduced completion activity and restructured contracts as a result of the Chapter 11 Cases.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our lease operating expenses on a BOE basis also decreased when comparing the Combined Current YTD Period to the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;LOE per BOE amounted to $6.43 during the Combined Current YTD Period, which represents a decrease of $0.74 per BOE (or 10%) from the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;This decrease was mainly due to the overall decrease in LOE expense discussed above, partially offset by lower overall production volumes between periods.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Transportation, Gathering, Compression and Other. </i> Our transportation, gathering, compression and other expenses (&#8220;TGC&#8221;) during the Combined Current YTD Period were $30 million, a $12 million decrease over the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. This decrease primarily relates to lower production volumes and decreased rates negotiated with midstream partners as a result of the Chapter 11 Cases. &#160;Additionally, during the Combined Current YTD Period, certain oil volumes that are typically transported by pipeline were instead transported by truck. &#160;Trucking fees are recorded as a reduction to the oil price received and not as TGC expense as control transfers prior to transport.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">TGC on a BOE basis also decreased when comparing the Combined Current YTD Period to the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. TGC per BOE amounted to $0.84 during the Combined Current YTD Period, which represents a decrease of $0.09 per BOE (or 10%) from the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;This decrease was primarily due to decreased rates negotiated with midstream partners and additional volumes being trucked during the Combined Current YTD Period as described above.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Production and Ad Valorem Taxes</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>Our production and ad valorem taxes during the Combined Current YTD Period were $65 million, a $73 million decrease compared to the Prior Predecessor YTD Period, which was primarily due to lower sales revenue between periods. &#160;Our production taxes are generally calculated as a percentage of net sales revenue before the effects of hedging, and this percentage on a company-wide basis was 8.5% and 8.6% for the Combined Current YTD Period and Prior Predecessor YTD Period, respectively. &#160;</p></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div style="display:table-cell;vertical-align:bottom;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:center;margin:24pt 0pt 0pt 0pt;">56</p></div></div></div>

compared to the Prior Predecessor YTD Period primarily due to cost reduction initiatives instituted beginning in the third quarter of 2019 and two separate company restructurings in August 2019 and September 2020, resulting in $40 million of lower compensation costs and $25 million of lower corporate overhead between periods. &#160;Costs related to litigation settlements also decreased $6 million between periods. &#160;These decreases were partially offset by $22 million paid to Predecessor executives and directors as cash retention incentives during the Combined Current YTD Period and $11 million of third-party advisory and legal fees related to the Chapter 11 Cases that were incurred prior to the Petition Date or after the Emergence Date. &#160;In addition, we incurred $8 million of severance and restructuring costs in both the Combined Current YTD Period and Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;The decrease in reimbursements and allocations for the Combined Current YTD Period was the result of a lower number of field workers on Whiting-operated properties associated with reduced drilling activity and staffing reductions. &#160;</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">G&amp;A expense per BOE amounted to $3.15 during the Combined Current YTD Period, which represents an increase of $0.26 per BOE (or 9%) from the $2.89 per BOE during the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;This increase was mainly due to the significant cost drivers discussed above, which added G&amp;A expenses of $1.26 per BOE and $0.41 per BOE for the Combined Current YTD Period and the Prior Predecessor YTD Period, respectively, as well as lower overall production volumes between periods. &#160;G&amp;A expense per BOE excluding such significant cost drivers was $1.89 per BOE and $2.48 per BOE for the Combined Current YTD Period and the Prior Predecessor YTD period, respectively. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Derivative (Gain) Loss, Net. &#160;</i>Our commodity derivative contracts are marked to market each reporting period with fair value gains and losses recognized immediately in earnings as derivative (gain) loss, net. &#160;Cash flow, however, is only impacted to the extent that settlements under these contracts result in making or receiving a payment to or from the counterparty. &#160;Derivative (gain) loss, net, amounted to a gain of $157 million and a loss of $54 million for the Combined Current YTD Period and Prior Predecessor YTD Period, respectively. &#160;These gains and losses relate to our collar and swap commodity derivative contracts and resulted from the downward and upward shifts, respectively, in the futures curve of forecasted commodity prices for crude oil and natural gas during the respective periods. &#160;For more information on our outstanding derivatives refer to the &#8220;Derivative Financial Instruments&#8221; footnote in the notes to the consolidated financial statements.</p></div><div gain on extinguishment of debt. &#160;Additionally, in September and October 2019, we paid $96 million to repurchase $100 million aggregate principal amount of our 5.75% Senior Notes due 2021 and and &#8220;Fresh Start Accounting&#8221; footnotes in the notes to the consolidated financial statements for more information on the legal restructuring and related Canadian deferred tax liability. &#160;</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">As a result of the full valuation allowance on our U.S. DTAs as of December&#160;31, 2020, August&#160;31, 2020 and December 31, 2019, no U.S. tax benefit or expense was recognized in the Combined Current YTD Period or the Prior Predecessor YTD Period other than a $1 million U.S. income tax benefit related to alternative minimum tax refunds received in each respective period. &#160;</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our overall effective tax rate of 1.7% and (42.7%) for the Combined Current YTD Period and the Prior Predecessor YTD Period, respectively, were lower than the U.S. statutory income tax rate as a result of the full valuation allowance on our U.S. DTAs and changes to our expected Canadian tax liability during each period as discussed above. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Year Ended December&#160;31, 2019 Compared to&#160;Year Ended December&#160;31, 2018</i></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">For discussion on the year ended December 31, 2019 (Predecessor) compared to the year ended December&#160;31, 2018 (Predecessor), refer to Part II, Item 7 &#8220;Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#8221; equity, while at December&#160;31, 2019, the Predecessor entity had $9&#160;million of cash on hand, $2.8 billion of long-term debt and $4.0 billion of equity. &#160;The decrease in long-term debt and shareholders&#8217; equity between periods primarily relates to adjustments made as a result of the implementation of the Plan and application of fresh start accounting upon emergence from bankruptcy on September&#160;1, 2020. &#160;We expect that our liquidity going forward will be primarily derived from cash flows from operating activities, cash on hand and availability under the Exit Credit Agreement and that these sources of liquidity will be sufficient to provide us the ability to fund our operating and development activities and planned capital programs. &#160;We may need to fund acquisitions or pursuits of business opportunities that support our strategy through additional borrowings or the issuance of common stock or other forms of equity.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Cash Flows. &#160;</i>During the Combined Current YTD Period, we generated $195 million of cash provided by operating activities, a decrease of $561 million from the Prior Predecessor YTD Period. &#160;Cash provided by operating activities between periods decreased primarily due to lower realized sales prices and production volumes for oil, NGLs and natural gas, as well as higher cash reorganization expenses. &#160;These negative factors were partially offset by an increase in cash settlements received on our derivative contracts and lower lease operating expenses, production and ad valorem taxes, cash G&amp;A, cash interest expense and TGC between periods. &#160;Refer to &#8220;Results of Operations&#8221; for more information on the impact of volumes and prices on revenues and for more information on increases and decreases in certain expenses between periods. &#160;During the Current Predecessor YTD Period, cash flows from operating activities, $425 million of net borrowings under the Exit Credit Agreement and $29 million of proceeds from the sale of properties were used to finance the repayment of $217 million of net borrowings under the Predecessor Credit Agreement, $238 million of drilling and development expenditures and the repurchase of $73 million aggregate principal amount of Senior Convertible Notes in March 2020. &#160;During the Successor Period, cash on hand and cash flows from operating activities were used to finance the repayment of $65 million of outstanding borrowings under the Exit Credit Agreement and $34 million of drilling and development expenditures.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">For discussion on cash flows for the year ended December 31, 2019 (Predecessor) compared to the year ended December&#160;31, 2018 (Predecessor), refer to Part II, Item 7 &#8220;Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of &#160;Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#8221; under the Exit Credit Agreement) and flexibility to modify future capital expenditure programs, we expect to fund all planned capital programs, comply with our debt covenants and meet other obligations that may arise from our oil and gas operations.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Exit Credit Agreement</i>. &#160;On September&#160;1, 2020, Whiting Petroleum Corporation, as parent guarantor, and Whiting Oil and Gas, as borrower, entered into the Exit Credit Agreement with a syndicate of banks<span style="background-color:#ffffff;">. &#160;As of December&#160;31, 2020, the Exit Credit Agreement had a borrowing base and aggregate commitments of $750&#160;million. &#160;As of December&#160;31, 2020, we had $388&#160;million of available borrowing capacity under the Exit Credit Agreement, which was net of $360&#160;million of borrowings outstanding and $2</span>&#160;million in letters of credit outstanding. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">The borrowing base under the Exit Credit Agreement is determined at the discretion of the lenders, based on the collateral value of our proved reserves that have been mortgaged to such lenders, and is subject to initial redetermination on April&#160;1, 2021, regular redeterminations on April&#160;1 and October&#160;1 of each year thereafter, as well as special redeterminations described in the Exit Credit Agreement, in each case which may increase or decrease the amount of the borrowing base. &#160;Additionally, we can increase the aggregate commitments <span style="background-color:#ffffff;">by up to an additional $750&#160;million, subject to certain conditions.</span></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;padding-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt;">A portion of the revolving credit facility in an aggregate amount not to exceed $50&#160;million may be used to issue letters of credit for the account of Whiting Oil and Gas or our other designated subsidiaries. &#160;As of December&#160;31, 2020, $48&#160;million was available for additional letters of credit under the Exit Credit Agreement.</p><p style="background-color:#ffffff;font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;padding-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt;">The Exit Credit Agreement provides for interest only payments until maturity on April 1, 2024, when the agreement terminates and all outstanding borrowings are due. In addition, the Exit Credit Agreement provides for certain mandatory prepayments, including if our cash balances are in excess of approximately $75&#160;million during any given week, such excess must be utilized to repay borrowings under the Exit Credit Agreement. &#160;Interest under the Exit Credit Agreement accrues at our option at either (i)&#160;a base rate for a base rate loan plus a margin between&#160;1.75% and&#160;2.75% based on the ratio of outstanding borrowings and letters of credit to the lower of the current borrowing base or total commitments, where the base rate is defined as the greatest of the prime rate, the federal funds rate plus&#160;0.5% per annum, or an adjusted LIBOR plus&#160;1.0% per annum, or (ii)&#160;an adjusted LIBOR for a eurodollar loan plus a margin between&#160;2.75% and&#160;3.75% based on the ratio of outstanding borrowings and letters of credit to the lower of the current borrowing base or total commitments. &#160;Additionally, we incur commitment fees of&#160;0.5% on the unused portion of the aggregate commitments of the lenders under the Exit Credit Agreement, which fees are included as a component of interest expense.</p></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div style="display:table-cell;vertical-align:bottom;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:center;margin:12pt 0pt 0pt 0pt;">61</p></div></div></div>

in the notes to the consolidated financial statements for more information.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our discussion of financial condition and results of operations is based upon the information reported in our consolidated financial statements. &#160;The preparation of these statements in accordance with GAAP and SEC rules and regulations requires us to make certain assumptions and estimates that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses as well as the disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of our financial statements. &#160;We base our assumptions and estimates on historical experience and other sources that we believe to be reasonable at the time. &#160;Actual results may vary from our estimates due to changes in circumstances, weather, political environment, global economics, mechanical problems, general business conditions and other factors. &#160;A summary of our significant accounting policies is detailed in the &#8220;Summary of Significant Policies&#8221; footnote in the notes to the consolidated financial statements. &#160;We have outlined below certain of these policies as being of particular importance to the portrayal of our financial position and results of operations and which require the application of significant judgment by our management.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Successful Efforts Accounting</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>We account for our oil and gas operations using the successful efforts method of accounting. &#160;Under this method, the fair value of property acquired and all costs associated with successful exploratory wells and all development wells are capitalized. &#160;Items charged to expense generally include geological and geophysical costs, costs of unsuccessful exploratory wells and oil and gas production costs. &#160;All of our properties are located within the continental United States.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Oil and Natural Gas Reserve Quantities</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>Reserve quantities and the related estimates of future net cash flows affect our periodic calculations of depletion, impairment of our oil and natural gas properties and our asset retirement obligations. &#160;Discounted future net cash flows derived from our reserve estimates were also utilized in establishing the fair value of our oil and natural gas properties upon the adoption of fresh start accounting on the Emergence Date. &#160;Proved oil and gas reserves are those quantities of oil and gas which, by analysis of geoscience and engineering data, can be estimated with reasonable certainty to be economically producible&#8212;from a given date forward, from known reservoirs and under existing economic conditions, operating methods, and government regulations&#8212;prior to the time at which contracts providing the right to operate expire, unless evidence indicates that renewal is reasonably certain, regardless of whether deterministic or probabilistic methods are used for the estimation. &#160;Reserve quantities and future cash flows included in this report are prepared in accordance with guidelines established by the SEC and the FASB. &#160;The accuracy of our reserve estimates is a function of (i)&#160;the quality and quantity of available data, (ii)&#160;the interpretation of that data, (iii)&#160;the accuracy of various mandated economic assumptions, and (iv)&#160;the judgments of the persons preparing the estimates.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt;">Our total proved reserves decreased 225 MMBOE, or 46%, from December 31, 2019 to December 31, 2020. &#160;Refer to &#8220;Reserves&#8221; in Item 2 and &#8220;Supplemental Disclosures about Oil and Gas Producing Activities&#8221; in Item 8 of this Annual Report on Form 10-K for information on the change in reserves between periods. &#160;External petroleum engineers independently estimated all of the proved reserve quantities included in this Annual Report on Form&#160;10-K. &#160;In connection with our external petroleum engineers performing their independent reserve estimations, we furnish them with the following information that they use in their evaluation: (1)&#160;technical support data, (2)&#160;technical analysis of geologic and engineering support information, (3)&#160;economic and production data, (4)&#160;our well ownership interests and (5) expected future development activity. &#160;The independent petroleum engineers, Netherland, Sewell &amp; Associates, Inc., evaluated 100% of our estimated proved reserve quantities and their related pre-tax future net cash flows as of December&#160;31, 2020. &#160;Estimates prepared by others may be higher or lower than our estimates. &#160;Because these estimates depend on many assumptions, all of which may differ substantially from actual results, reserve estimates may be different from the quantities of oil and gas that are ultimately </p></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div style="display:table-cell;vertical-align:bottom;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:center;margin:24pt 0pt 0pt 0pt;">62</p></div></div></div>

style="max-width:100%;padding-left:5.88%;padding-right:5.88%;position:relative;"><div style="margin-top:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt;"><a href="#TOC"><span style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;text-align:left;">Table of Contents</span></a></p></div><div style="clear:both;max-width:100%;position:relative;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">recovered. &#160;For example, if the crude oil and natural gas prices used in our year-end reserve estimates increased or decreased by 10%, our proved reserve quantities at December&#160;31, 2020 would have increased by 17&#160;MMBOE (6%) or decreased by 29&#160;MMBOE (11%), respectively, and the pre-tax PV10% of our proved reserves would have increased by $393 million (33%) or decreased by $352 million (29%), respectively. &#160;We continually make revisions to reserve estimates throughout the&#160;year as additional information becomes available. &#160;We make changes to depletion rates and impairment calculations (when impairment indicators arise) in the same period that changes to reserve estimates are made.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Depreciation, Depletion and Amortization. &#160;</i>Our rate of recording DD&amp;A is dependent upon our estimates of total proved and proved developed reserves, which estimates incorporate various assumptions and future projections. &#160;If our estimates of total proved or proved developed reserves decline, the rate at which we record DD&amp;A expense increases, which in turn reduces our net income. &#160;Such a decline in reserves may result from lower commodity prices or other changes to reserve estimates, as discussed above, and we are unable to predict changes in reserve quantity estimates as such quantities are dependent on the success of our exploration and development program, as well as future economic conditions. &#160;Our DD&amp;A rate declined significantly during the Successor Period as compared to both the Current Predecessor YTD Period and Prior Predecessor YTD Period as a result of our adoption of fresh start accounting on the Emergence Date, which resulted in a reduced book value of our oil and natural gas properties at that date as compared to either Predecessor period.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Impairment of Oil and Gas Properties</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>We review the value of our oil and gas properties whenever management judges that events and circumstances indicate that the recorded carrying value of properties may not be recoverable. &#160;Such events and circumstances include, but are not limited to, declines in commodity prices, increases in operating costs, unfavorable reserve revisions, poor well performance, changes in development plans and potential property divestitures. &#160;Impairments of producing properties are determined by comparing their undiscounted future net cash flows to their net book values at the end of each period. &#160;If a property&#8217;s net capitalized costs exceed undiscounted future net cash flows, the cost of the property is written down to &#8220;fair value,&#8221; which is determined using discounted future net cash flows from the producing property. &#160;Different pricing assumptions or discount rates could result in a different calculated impairment. &#160;In addition to proved property impairments, we provide for impairments on significant undeveloped properties when we determine that the property will not be developed or a permanent impairment in value has occurred. &#160;Individually insignificant unproved properties are amortized on a composite basis, based on past success, experience and average remaining lease-term.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Asset Retirement Obligation. &#160;</i>Our asset retirement obligations (&#8220;ARO&#8221;) consist of estimated future costs associated with the plugging and abandonment of oil and gas wells, removal of equipment and facilities from leased acreage and land restoration in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws and the terms of our lease agreements. &#160;The discounted fair value of an ARO liability is required to be recognized in the period in which it is incurred, with the associated asset retirement cost capitalized as part of the carrying cost of the oil and gas asset. &#160;The recognition of an ARO requires that management make numerous assumptions regarding such factors as the estimated probabilities, amounts and timing of settlements; the credit-adjusted risk-free discount rate; the inflation rate; and future advances in technology. &#160;In periods subsequent to the initial measurement of an ARO, we must recognize period-to-period changes in the liability resulting from the passage of time and revisions to either the timing or the amount of the original estimate of undiscounted cash flows. &#160;Increases in the ARO liability due to the passage of time impact net income as accretion expense. &#160;The related capitalized cost, including revisions thereto, is charged to expense through DD&amp;A over the life of the oil and gas property.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Derivative Instruments</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>All derivative instruments are recorded in the consolidated financial statements at fair value, other than derivative instruments that meet the &#8220;normal purchase normal sale&#8221; exclusion or other derivative scope exceptions. &#160;We do not currently apply hedge accounting to any of our outstanding derivative instruments, and as a result, all changes in derivative fair values are recognized currently in earnings.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">We determine the recorded amounts of our derivative instruments measured at fair value utilizing third-party valuation specialists. &#160;We review these valuations, including the related model inputs and assumptions, and analyze changes in fair value measurements between periods. &#160;We corroborate such inputs, calculations and fair value changes using various methodologies, and review unobservable inputs for reasonableness utilizing relevant information from other published sources. &#160;When available, we utilize counterparty valuations to assess the reasonableness of our valuations. &#160;The values we report in our financial statements change as the assumptions used in these valuations are revised to reflect changes in market conditions (particularly those for oil and natural gas futures) or other factors, many of which are beyond our control.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">We periodically, and are currently contractually obligated under the Exit Credit Agreement to, enter into commodity derivative contracts to manage our exposure to oil and natural gas price volatility. &#160;We primarily utilize costless collars and swaps which are generally placed with major financial institutions, as well as crude oil sales and delivery contracts. &#160;We use hedging to help ensure that we have adequate funding for our capital programs and to manage returns on our drilling programs and acquisitions. &#160;Our decision on the quantity and price at which we choose to hedge our production is based in part on our view of current and future market conditions. &#160;While the use of these hedging arrangements limits the downside risk of adverse price movements, it may also limit future revenues from favorable price movements. &#160;The use of hedging transactions also involves the risk that the counterparties will be unable to meet the financial terms of such transactions. &#160;We evaluate the ability of our counterparties to perform at the inception of a hedging relationship and on a periodic basis as appropriate.</p></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div style="display:table-cell;vertical-align:bottom;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:center;margin:24pt 0pt 0pt 0pt;">63</p></div></div></div>
<div style="background-color:#000000;clear:both;height:2pt;page-break-after:always;width:88.24%;border:0;margin:30pt 5.88% 30pt 5.88%;"></div><div style="max-width:100%;padding-left:5.88%;padding-right:5.88%;position:relative;"><div style="margin-top:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt;"><a href="#TOC"><span style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;text-align:left;">Table of Contents</span></a></p></div><div style="clear:both;max-width:100%;position:relative;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">We value our collars and swaps using industry-standard models that consider various assumptions, including quoted forward prices for commodities, time value, volatility factors and contractual prices for the underlying instruments, as well as other relevant economic measures. &#160;We value our long-term crude oil sales and delivery contracts based on a probability-weighted income approach which considers various assumptions, including quoted spot prices for commodities, market differentials for crude oil and U.S. Treasury rates. &#160;The discount rates used in the fair values of these instruments include a measure of nonperformance risk by the counterparty or us, as appropriate.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">In addition, we evaluate the terms of our contracts, if any, to determine whether they contain embedded components that are required to be bifurcated and accounted for separately as derivative financial instruments.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Income Taxes and Uncertain Tax Positions</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>We provide for income taxes in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 740 &#8211; <i style="font-style:italic;">Income Taxes </i>(&#8220;ASC 740&#8221;). &#160;We record deferred tax assets and liabilities to account for the expected future tax consequences of events that have been recognized in our financial statements and our tax returns. &#160;We routinely assess the realizability of our deferred tax assets. &#160;If we conclude that it is more likely than not that some portion or all of our deferred tax assets will not be realized, the tax asset is reduced by a valuation allowance. &#160;We consider future taxable income in making such assessments. &#160;Numerous judgments and assumptions are inherent in the determination of future taxable income, including factors such as future operating conditions, particularly as they relate to prevailing oil and natural gas prices.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Internal Revenue Code (&#8220;IRC&#8221;) Section 382 addresses company ownership changes and specifically limits the utilization of certain deductions and other tax attributes on an annual basis following an ownership change. &#160;As a result of the Chapter 11 reorganization and related transactions, the Successor experienced an ownership change within the meaning of IRC Section 382 on the Emergence Date. &#160;This ownership change subjected certain of the Company&#8217;s tax attributes to an IRC Section 382 limitation. &#160;This limitation has not resulted in a current tax liability for the Successor Period, or any intervening period since the Emergence Date. &#160;The ownership changes and resulting annual limitation may result in the expiration of net operating loss carryforwards or other tax attributes otherwise available, with a corresponding decrease in the Company&#8217;s valuation allowance.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">ASC 740 requires uncertain income tax positions to meet a more-likely-than-not realization threshold to be recognized in the financial statements. &#160;Under ASC 740, uncertain tax positions that previously failed to meet the more-likely-than-not threshold should be recognized in the first subsequent financial reporting period in which that threshold is met. &#160;Previously recognized uncertain tax positions that no longer meet the more-likely-than-not threshold should be derecognized in the first subsequent financial reporting period in which that threshold is no longer met.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">We are subject to taxation in many jurisdictions, and the calculation of our tax liabilities involves dealing with uncertainties in the application of complex tax laws and regulations in various taxing jurisdictions. &#160;If we ultimately determine that the payment of these liabilities will be unnecessary, we reverse the liability and recognize a tax benefit during the period in which we determine the liability no longer applies. &#160;Conversely, we record additional tax charges in a period in which we determine that a recorded tax liability is less than we expect the ultimate assessment to be.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Revenue Recognition</i>. &#160;We predominantly derive our revenue from the sale of produced oil, NGLs and natural gas. &#160;Revenue is recognized when we meet our performance obligation to deliver the product and control is transferred to the customer. &#160;We receive payment for product sales from one to three months after delivery. &#160;At the end of each month when the performance obligation is satisfied, the amount of production delivered and the price we will receive can be reasonably estimated and amounts due from customers are accrued in accounts receivable trade, net in the consolidated balance sheets. &#160;Variances between our estimated revenue and actual payments are recorded in the&#160;month the payment is received. &#160;However, differences have been and are insignificant.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Accounting for Business Combinations</i>.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i>We account for business combinations using the acquisition method, which is the only method permitted under FASB ASC Topic 805 &#8211; <i style="font-style:italic;">Business Combinations</i>, and involves the use of significant judgment.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Under the acquisition method of accounting, a business combination is accounted for at a purchase price based upon the fair value of the consideration given. &#160;The assets and liabilities acquired are measured at their fair values, and the purchase price is allocated to the assets and liabilities based upon these fair values. &#160;The excess, if any, of the consideration given to acquire an entity over the net amounts assigned to its assets acquired and liabilities assumed is recognized as goodwill. &#160;The excess, if any, of the fair value of assets acquired and liabilities assumed over the cost of an acquired entity is recognized immediately to earnings as a gain from bargain purchase.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Determining the fair values of the assets and liabilities acquired involves the use of judgment, since some of the assets and liabilities acquired do not have fair values that are readily determinable. &#160;Different techniques may be used to determine fair values, including market prices (where available), appraisals, comparisons to transactions for similar assets and liabilities, and present values of estimated future cash flows, among others. &#160;Since these estimates involve the use of significant judgment, they can change as new information becomes available.</p></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div style="display:table-cell;vertical-align:bottom;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:center;margin:24pt 0pt 0pt 0pt;">64</p></div></div></div>
<div style="background-color:#000000;clear:both;height:2pt;page-break-after:always;width:88.24%;border:0;margin:30pt 5.88% 30pt 5.88%;"></div><div style="max-width:100%;padding-left:5.88%;padding-right:5.88%;position:relative;"><div style="margin-top:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt;"><a href="#TOC"><span style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;text-align:left;">Table of Contents</span></a></p></div><div style="clear:both;max-width:100%;position:relative;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">The business combinations completed during the prior three&#160;years consisted of oil and gas properties. &#160;In general, the consideration we have paid to acquire these properties or companies was entirely allocated to the fair value of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed at the time of acquisition and consequently, there was no goodwill nor any bargain purchase gains recognized on our business combinations.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Leases. &#160;</i>We have operating and finance leases for corporate and field offices, pipeline and midstream facilities, field equipment and automobiles. &#160;Right-of-use (&#8220;ROU&#8221;) assets and liabilities associated with these leases are recognized at the lease commencement date based on the present value of the lease payments over the lease term. &#160;ROU assets represent our right to use an underlying asset for the lease term, and lease liabilities represent our obligation to make lease payments. &#160;Upon adoption of fresh start accounting, our remaining lease obligations were recalculated using the applicable incremental borrowing rate commensurate with the Successor&#39;s capital structure upon emergence.<i style="font-style:italic;"> &#160;</i></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Operating lease cost is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term. &#160;Finance lease cost is recognized based on the effective interest method for the lease liability and straight-line amortization of the ROU asset, resulting in more cost being recognized in earlier lease periods. &#160;All payments for short-term leases, including leases with a term of one month or less, are recognized in income or capitalized to the cost of oil and gas properties on a straight-line basis over the lease term. &#160;Additionally, any variable payments, which are generally related to the corresponding utilization of the asset, are recognized in the period in which the obligation was incurred. </p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Reorganization and Fresh Start Accounting</i>. &#160;Effective April 1, 2020, as a result of the filing of the Chapter 11 Cases we began accounting and reporting according to FASB ASC Topic 852 &#8211; <i style="font-style:italic;">Reorganizations </i>(&#8220;ASC 852&#8221;), which specifies the accounting and financial reporting requirements for entities reorganizing through chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. &#160;These requirements include distinguishing transactions associated with the reorganization and implementation of the plan of reorganization separate from activities related to ongoing operations of the business. &#160;Additionally upon emergence from the Chapter 11 Cases, ASC 852 requires us to allocate our reorganization value to our individual assets based on their estimated fair values, resulting in a new entity for financial reporting purposes. &#160;After the Emergence Date, the accounting and reporting requirements of ASC 852 are no longer applicable and have no impact on the Successor periods.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Effects of Inflation and Pricing</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">As commodity prices began to recover during 2018 and 2019 from previous lows, the cost of oil field goods and services also rose. &#160;Although commodity prices declined sharply during the first part of 2020, the costs of oil field goods and services were slower to decline in response. &#160;The oil and gas industry is very cyclical, and the demand for goods and services of oil field companies, suppliers and others associated with the industry puts extreme pressure on the economic stability and pricing structure within the industry. &#160;Typically, as prices for oil and natural gas increase, so do all associated costs. &#160;Conversely, in a period of declining prices, associated cost declines are likely to lag and not adjust downward in proportion to prices. &#160;Material changes in prices also impact our current revenue stream, estimates of future reserves, borrowing base calculations of bank loans, depletion expense, impairment assessments of oil and gas properties and values of properties in purchase and sale transactions. &#160;Material changes in prices can impact the value of oil and gas companies and their ability to raise capital, borrow money and retain personnel. &#160;While we do not currently expect business costs to materially increase in the near term, higher demand in the industry could result in increases in the costs of materials, services and personnel.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Forward-Looking Statements</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">This report contains statements that we believe to be &#8220;forward-looking statements&#8221; within the meaning of <div style="background-color:#000000;clear:both;height:2pt;page-break-after:always;width:88.24%;border:0;margin:30pt 5.88% 30pt 5.88%;"></div><div style="max-width:100%;padding-left:5.88%;padding-right:5.88%;position:relative;"><div style="margin-top:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt;"><a href="#TOC"><span style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;text-align:left;">Table of Contents</span></a></p></div><div style="clear:both;max-width:100%;position:relative;"><a id="Item7AQuantitativeandQualitativeDisclosu"></a><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Item&#160;7A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;<b style="font-weight:bold;text-decoration:underline;text-decoration-color:#000000;">Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk</b></p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Commodity Price Risk</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">The price we receive for our oil, NGL and gas production heavily influences our revenue, profitability, access to capital and future rate of growth. &#160;Crude oil and natural gas are commodities, and therefore, their prices are subject to wide fluctuations in response to relatively minor changes in supply and demand. &#160;Historically, the markets for oil, NGLs and gas have been volatile, and these markets will likely continue to be volatile in the future. &#160;</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">We periodically enter into derivative contracts to achieve a more predictable cash flow by reducing our exposure to oil and natural gas price volatility. &#160;Our derivative contracts have traditionally been costless collars and swaps, although we evaluate and have entered into other forms of derivative instruments as well. &#160;Currently, we do not apply hedge accounting, and therefore all changes in commodity derivative fair values are recorded immediately to earnings.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;"><i style="font-style:italic;">Crude Oil and Natural Gas Collars and Swaps. &#160;</i>Our hedging portfolio currently consists of crude oil and natural gas collars and swaps. &#160;Refer to the &#8220;Derivative Financial Instruments&#8221; footnote in the notes to the consolidated financial statements for a description and list of our outstanding derivative contracts at December&#160;31, 2020.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Our collar contracts have the effect of providing a protective floor, while allowing us to share in upward pricing movements up to the ceiling price. &#160;Our swap contracts entitle us to receive settlement from the counterparty in amounts, if any, by which the settlement price for the applicable calculation period is less than the fixed price, or to pay the counterparty if the settlement price for the applicable calculation period is more than the fixed price. &#160;The fair value of our oil derivative positions at December&#160;31, 2020 was a net liability of $60 million. &#160;A hypothetical upward or downward shift of 10% per Bbl in the NYMEX forward curve for crude oil as of December&#160;31, 2020 would cause an increase of $67 million or a decrease of $60 million, respectively, in this fair value liability. &#160;The fair value of our natural gas contracts was a net asset of $1 million. &#160;A hypothetical upward or downward shift of 10% per MMBtu in the NYMEX forward curve for natural gas as of December&#160;31, 2020 would cause a decrease or an increase, respectively, of $8 million in this fair value asset.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">While these collars and fixed-price swaps are designed to decrease our exposure to downward price movements, they also have the effect of limiting the benefit of price increases above the ceiling with respect to the collars and upward price movements generally with respect to the fixed-price swaps.</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold;margin:12pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Interest Rate Risk</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:justify;margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 0pt;">Market risk is estimated as the change in fair value resulting from a hypothetical 100 basis point change in the interest rate on the outstanding balance under the Exit Credit Agreement. &#160;The Exit Credit Agreement allows us to fix the interest rate for all or a portion of the principal balance for a period up to one month. &#160;To the extent that the interest rate is fixed, interest rate changes affect the instrument&#8217;s fair market value but do not impact results of operations or cash flows. &#160;Conversely, for the portion of the Exit Credit Agreement that has a floating interest rate, interest rate changes will not affect the fair market value but will impact future results of operations and cash flows. &#160;At December&#160;31, 2020, our outstanding principal balance under the Exit Credit Agreement was $360 million, and the weighted average interest rate on the outstanding principal balance was 4.1%. &#160;At December&#160;31, 2020, the carrying amount approximated fair market value. &#160;Assuming a constant debt level of $360 million, the cash flow impact resulting from a 100 basis point change in interest rates during periods when the interest rate is not fixed would be $3 million over a 12-month time period. &#160;</p><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;margin:0pt;"><span style="visibility:hidden;">&#8203;</span></p><a id="_39053e38_f91a_47c0_aa8b_461f4230f66b"></a></div><div style="clear:both;display:table;margin-bottom:14.4pt;min-height:21.6pt;width:100%;"><div style="display:table-cell;vertical-align:bottom;width:100%;"><p style="font-family:'Times New Roman','Times','serif';font-size:10pt;text-align:center;margin:24pt 0pt 0pt 0pt;">67</p></div></div></div>
